# Education in Greece
Education in Greece is structured into preschool (ages 4–6), primary (ages 6–12), lower secondary (Gymnasium, ages 12–15), and upper secondary education (Lyceum, ages 15–18). Preschool is compulsory, lasts two years, and includes Pre-kindergarten and Kindergarten, with English introduced early as a core subject. Primary education is compulsory for six years and culminates in the "Apolytirio Dimotikou" certificate. Lower secondary Gymnasium is also compulsory, lasting three years, leading to the "Apolytirio Gymnasium" certificate required for entry into upper secondary education. Lyceum is non-compulsory, lasts three years, and concludes with the "Apolytirio Lykeiou," a prerequisite for higher education entrance examinations ("Pan-Hellenic Examinations"). Secondary education includes various specialized and vocational schools, such as Vocational Lyceums (EPAL), Music, Art, Model, Special, and Experimental schools. Vocational education offers dual diplomas combining academic qualification and vocational training, with post-lyceum apprenticeship options. Public Onassis Schools target socially challenged areas with free attendance and admission exams. Since 2026–2027, select public schools will also offer the English-taught International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme. The National Qualifications Framework (HQF) aligns education levels from primary (level 1) through tertiary education (levels 6–8). Higher education includes public and authorized private institutions, offering tuition-free undergraduate studies, with some postgraduate programs requiring fees.
The Greek education system emphasizes continuous assessment, foreign language instruction beginning in kindergarten, and diverse pathways including general academic and vocational tracks. National matriculation exams determine access to higher education, with specialized tests for artistic and technical fields. Several types of vocational and specialized secondary schools exist, supported by a national framework for certification and apprenticeship governed by the Ministry of Education and related bodies. Adult education and lifelong learning programs complement formal education, with digital platforms augmenting access. The system faces challenges including funding, corruption, and past disciplinary controversies but continues to evolve with new programs and reforms.
